LEARN

Learn how memory, retrieval, evidence, and structured context work.

Conceptual foundations, architectural trade-offs, and educational guides for developers building durable AI memory systems.

START HERE

Three foundational cornerstones.

If you are new to AI memory systems, start with these core conceptual guides.

Foundations

What is AI memory?

AI memory is the persistence layer that allows models and autonomous agents to retain state, recall verified past interactions, and accumulate knowledge across execution boundaries.

7 min readRead guide →
Foundations

RAG vs AI memory: What is the difference?

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fetches static reference material to ground prompt generation, whereas AI memory manages persistent, evolving agent and user state across time.

8 min readRead guide →
Evidence & Trust

What is evidence-aware memory?

Evidence-aware memory is an architectural paradigm where an AI system cannot store or recall an assertion without binding it to verifiable source identity, evidence spans, and authorization scopes.

8 min readRead guide →

Foundations

Core principles of state, memory boundaries, and representations in agent architectures.

Learn

What is AI memory?

AI memory is the persistence layer that allows models and autonomous agents to retain state, recall verified past interactions, and accumulate knowledge across execution boundaries.

7 min readRead →

Learn

RAG vs AI memory: What is the difference?

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fetches static reference material to ground prompt generation, whereas AI memory manages persistent, evolving agent and user state across time.

8 min readRead →

Learn

Structured memory vs unstructured memory

Unstructured memory stores raw text snippets and embeddings, while structured memory organizes knowledge into typed assertions, entities, relations, and explicit schemas.

8 min readRead →

Memory & Retrieval

Vector similarity, lexical BM25, graph traversals, and hybrid fusion mechanics.

Learn

What is semantic search?

Semantic search retrieves information by estimated meaning and context, not only by exact word overlap.

6 min readRead →

Learn

Why vector search alone is not enough for agent memory

Vector search excels at conceptual similarity over unstructured text, but agent memory requires exact identifiers, relational joins, temporal validity, and strict authorization.

8 min readRead →

Learn

Hybrid retrieval explained: Vector search, lexical search, and structured signals

Hybrid retrieval combines dense vector embeddings, sparse lexical inverted indexes (BM25), and structured database filters to prevent single-strategy retrieval failures.

9 min readRead →

Learn

Why graphs matter in AI memory

Knowledge graphs represent entities and their explicit relationships, allowing AI agents to navigate multi-hop connections and topological context that flat chunk search cannot resolve.

8 min readRead →

Learn

What is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)?

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines ranked lists from multiple search algorithms into a single unified result set without requiring fragile score normalization.

7 min readRead →

Evidence & Trust

Provenance records, source anchoring, authorization scopes, and verifiable auditability.

Learn

What is evidence-aware memory?

Evidence-aware memory is an architectural paradigm where an AI system cannot store or recall an assertion without binding it to verifiable source identity, evidence spans, and authorization scopes.

8 min readRead →

Learn

What is provenance in AI systems?

Provenance is the complete, recorded history of information: its origin entity, ingestion transformations, supporting evidence spans, and authorization lifecycle.

7 min readRead →

Learn

Memory scope and authorization in multi-agent systems

Multi-agent systems require rigorous memory scoping across tenants, workspaces, agents, and temporal windows to prevent data leakage and cross-context contamination.

8 min readRead →
